references.text: The immediate context: The two disciples were on their way to Emmaus and talking with each other about all that had happened ([ref:Luk 24:14-15|Luke 24:14-15]). Jesus' question in verse 17 refers directly to this conversation.

Mary Magdalene also did not recognize the risen Jesus when he asked her a question: "Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you looking for?" ([ref:Joh 20:15|John 20:15]). Both events show that Jesus addressed grieving disciples without being recognized.

At the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus stood on the shore without the disciples realizing it was him, and he asked them if they had caught any fish ([ref:Joh 21:4-5|John 21:4-5]). Again, Jesus opens the conversation with a question without being recognized.
The reason they stood still with a sorrowful expression (σκυθρωποί) was that their eyes were kept from recognizing him ([ref:Luk 24:16|Luke 24:16]).

God asked Adam a question when he walked in the garden – "Where are you?" ([ref:1 Mos 3:9|Genesis 3:9]) – even though He already knew the answer. Similarly, Jesus asked the disciples what they were discussing, even though He knew it.

Daniel also describes one who came to explain a vision and asked questions to open up the conversation ([ref:Dan 8:17|Daniel 8:17]). God's messengers often begin revelations by addressing the grieving.

Earlier in the Gospel of Luke, Jesus asked the blind man: "What do you want me to do for you?" ([ref:Luk 18:40-41|Luke 18:40-41]). Jesus asked questions not because He lacked knowledge, but to invite the other person to express their need.

The expression σκυθρωποί (sorrowful/dark in face) also appears in Jesus' teaching on fasting, where he warns against being "σκυθρωποί" like the hypocrites ([ref:Matt 6:16|Matthew 6:16]). It is the same rare Greek word used here in Luke 24:17.
